text: The OSI model is a seven-layer conceptual framework, not a protocol you install — no vendor ships OSI, real networks run TCP/IP. But it gives everyone in a troubleshooting conversation a shared vocabulary for where a problem actually lives, before anyone has looked at a single packet. Bottom to top: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application — remembered with Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.

Each layer has a distinct job. Physical moves raw bits over cable or radio. Data Link adds MAC addressing and frame forwarding — switches operate here. Network adds IP addressing and routing — routers operate here. Transport handles end-to-end delivery between applications using port numbers, via TCP or UDP.

That Layer 2 versus Layer 3 distinction — switches forwarding by MAC address inside one network, routers forwarding by IP address between networks — is one of the most common things a working network professional is expected to know cold.

The real power of the model shows up in troubleshooting. When a user reports the internet is down, you work the layers bottom-up: is the cable connected, does the switch see the device's MAC address, does the device have a valid IP and can it reach its gateway, and finally, is there an application-level error like a DNS failure.
Next lesson: the TCP/IP model — the four-layer model real networks actually run — and exactly how its layers map onto the seven-layer OSI framework you just learned.
